Monday
Confession: I've been awful about Zubin in my head, and a bit out loud. The smell of his fish curry, his prayers at dawn with the incense, the way he dries clothes on every chair in our co-living flat. Yesterday I joked to Neeraja that our flat "smells like a fish-market temple". She laughed. I felt gross afterwards.
Tonight I made a list with two columns. Real problems: incense smoke drifting into my room at 5 a.m. and waking me; wet clothes on my desk chair. Just different: the fish, the prayers, his old songs. The second column isn't mine to fix. The first I can ask about like an adult.
So I knocked. "Could you keep your door shut when the incense is lit? The smoke comes straight into my room. And could my chair not be for drying?" He apologised and said he'd use the balcony stand. Then he offered me fish curry. I said next time. Maybe I'll actually mean it.
— Irawati

Okay, Bhavesh, you want the flat drama? For four months, Jeevan paid his rent share late. Five days, ten days. Every time, I covered it, said nothing, and then sat on my bed doing angry maths.
I didn't say anything because I didn't want to sound petty. So instead I went cold. Stopped cooking extra dal for him, didn't laugh at his jokes. He had no idea why.
Last month I finally said it over tea: "Jeevan, the rent's been late every month, and I've been covering it and getting quietly annoyed. Can we write down dates?" He went quiet. Then he told me his father's crop had failed in the rains, and he'd been too embarrassed to say.
So we made a note on the fridge: dates, amounts, who paid. And for this month, I told him to pay when the next harvest comes in. I've never seen him look so relieved.
So yes, that's me, Jatin, finally using my words.

In February my roommate Keerthana stopped going to class. She'd lie facing the wall till noon, skip dinner, and say "just tired" if I asked. The girls next door started whispering about her "drama". I almost joined in, just to have something to say.

Every Saturday Sofia folded sheets at her parents' laundry in Madrid, the laundry they had run for twenty years since arriving from Quito. Her mother's hands were cracked from hot water; her father still worked Sundays.
"They did all this so you could be a pharmacist," her cousin Dalia said, handing her a pile of towels. "You can't just switch to teaching."
Sofia pressed a crease flat. "I know what they gave up. I think about it every time I see Mamá's hands." She paused. "But if I choose pharmacy only to pay them back, I'll hate it, and they'll feel it."
"So you'll rebel?"
"No. I'll tell them the truth. That I'm grateful, and that teaching is what I'm good at."
That night she sat at the kitchen table with both parents and said exactly that. Her father was silent a long time. Her mother cried a little. Then her father asked, "Will you be happy?"
"Yes."
"Then show us the plan."

Afreen, final-year B.Com, came in upset. Her family has been sharing biodatas every weekend and arranged two "just tea" visits this month. She said she had been agreeing to each meeting "to end the conversation", then feeling trapped. She wants two years of work first.

Today she came back. She had spoken to her parents on Sunday. Her father worried about her "getting too old"; her mother worried about what relatives say. They agreed to pause visits until after her exams and talk again then. She looked tired, and much lighter.

Amma put another biodata next to my plate at lunch. Engineer, Chennai, "good family". The fifth since Pongal.

Appa asked what I'd look for in a person. Nobody has ever asked me that. I told him: kind, curious, not scared of my ambition. He nodded slowly.
Nothing's settled. But nobody slammed a door.

In the courtyard of her grandfather's house in Bhadohi, Trisha sat across from Mohan while both families drank tea under the neem tree. Mohan's mother listed his land, his tractor and his government job. Trisha's aunts nodded approvingly.
Her cousin Ganga nudged her. "Ask something. Anything."
Trisha took a breath. "Would you be all right with me continuing to teach at the school after marriage?"

That night, on the roof with Ganga, she said, "He's not a bad man. But he didn't ask me one thing. I'm going to tell Baba no." Ganga squeezed her hand. "Then say it tomorrow, calmly." In the morning she did. Her father sighed, but listened.

Ganga, beti, you're angry with your parents? Sit. Your Vijay Dada has a story about anger.
In 1974 I was twenty-one, in Jhansi. I wanted to join the Railways as a mechanic. My father wanted me in his cloth shop. He wouldn't even let me finish a sentence about it.
So I did the dramatic thing. I packed a tin trunk and told him, "If you won't listen, I'm leaving for Bombay tomorrow." He said, "Go, then." And I went, all the way to the bus stand, and sat there till midnight, too proud to go back and too scared to leave.
Your Dadi, only a neighbour then, found me and said, "Threats won't make him hear you."
A week later, calm, I sat beside him in the shop and said, "Babuji, I love you. I'm not good with cloth. I'm good with engines. Let me try for one year." He was quiet a long time. Then he said, "One year."
Anger is a messenger, beti. Let it deliver the message, then send it home.

When I was twenty, in Coimbatore, I found out he had lost his mill job a whole year before. Every morning he would put on his pressed shirt, take his tiffin, and sit in the temple library till five, then come home and ask about my exams. For a year.
I was furious. My hero, lying to all of us. For months I barely spoke to him, and when I did, it was with a sneer. "Going to office, Appa?" I said once. I still remember his face.
Then one night I found him at the kitchen table, counting coins for my college fees. He looked so small. And I understood: he wasn't a hero or a liar. He was a frightened man trying to protect us, badly.
I grieved for the father I'd imagined. Then I got to know the real one. He was worth knowing, Arohi. Yours are too.

qa.q: Where did Deepak's Appa spend his days after losing his job?
qa.a: In the temple library, till five.

qa.q: What did Deepak feel on finding out about the lost job?
qa.a: Furious and betrayed, treating his father with sneering contempt for months.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Deepak's story?
qa.a: Finding his father counting coins for Deepak's fees at the kitchen table, which showed a frightened man, not a hero or a liar.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt when Deepak asked "Going to office, Appa?"
qa.a: Ashamed and hurt, a look Deepak still remembers on his face.

grounding: Shows discovering a parent's flaws, the pull of contempt, and grieving the imagined hero to accept an imperfect parent who did his best.

subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
passage:
The generator at the wedding hall in Indore failed twice before dinner, and by the second time Papa was shouting at the young caterer in front of everyone: "Useless! Do you know who I am?"
Ankita stood frozen by the dessert counter. This was the man who had taught her to thank bus conductors. Now he was red-faced and boasting about his "contacts".
Her younger sister Bhavna rolled her eyes. "Your hero. Honestly, I'm done listening to anything he says."
Ankita felt something drop inside her, like a stair missing in the dark. She wanted to agree with Bhavna, to write him off entirely.
Instead she went and quietly apologised to the caterer, then found Papa by the stage. "That was unkind," she said. He blustered, then deflated. "I'm tired. Your Mausi's wedding... I'm scared of letting everyone down."
On the drive home, Ankita watched him doze against the window. Not a hero. Not a villain. Just her tired, flawed father. She felt sad, and oddly closer.

qa.q: How many times did the generator fail before dinner?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What did Ankita feel as she watched Papa shout at the caterer?
qa.a: Shocked and disillusioned, "like a stair missing in the dark", and tempted to write him off.

qa.q: What did Ankita do instead of writing her father off?
qa.a: She apologised to the caterer, told Papa plainly it was unkind, and listened to his fear, accepting him as flawed.

qa.q: How does Bhavna react to Papa's outburst?
qa.a: With contempt, deciding she is done listening to anything he says.

grounding: Illustrates seeing a parent as a flawed human, grieving the lost ideal and accepting him rather than turning to contempt.
